title: Painted journal cover
subtitle: Applying acrylic paint to a hardback journal cover for a personalised, durable finish
excerpt: A hardback journal cover painted in acrylics is much more durable than it sounds. Thin acrylic layers on book cloth or card board bend without cracking, and a final coat of acrylic medium seals the surface against abrasion and spills. The technique requires no special materials beyond the journal, basic acrylic paints, and a couple of flat brushes.
sourceNotes: Acrylic painting on bookbinding board and book cloth is a contemporary art journalling and bookbinding decorative technique. This entry is an original Homemade design.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin coat of clear acrylic medium (matte or satin) applied over a finished painted surface. The sealing coat protects the underlying paint from abrasion, moisture, and peeling, and binds any edges or seams in the design.

content.text: A painted hardback journal cover starts with two or three thin base coats of acrylic paint in your background colour. Thin is the key word: thick acrylic on a journal cover cracks at the hinge points where the cover flexes when the journal opens. Two or three thin coats (each thinned with water to a consistency slightly thinner than yoghurt) are more durable than one thick coat. Allow each coat to dry fully before adding the next.

items.name: Hardback journal, A5, cloth or card cover
items.notes: Book cloth (woven textile) covers take acrylic paint better than glossy laminate covers. If the cover has a laminate coating, sand very lightly with 220-grit sandpaper to give the paint surface a key.

items.name: Acrylic paints, 2 to 4 colours
items.notes: Standard artist or craft acrylic. No specialist 'fabric' paint needed for a journal cover.

items.name: Acrylic matte medium
items.notes: Dilute the paint and also use as a final sealing coat. Matte medium dries without gloss and will not obscure brushwork.

content.text: Thin the background colour acrylic with water and a small amount of matte medium until it flows easily off the brush in a thin stream. Apply the first coat across the entire cover surface in one direction. Allow to dry fully (20 to 30 minutes in a warm room). Apply a second coat in the opposite direction. Two coats of thinned acrylic over book cloth usually give full, even coverage. On card covers, three coats may be needed.

Sketch the design lightly in pencil on the dried base coat. Paint the design in layers from the largest areas to the finest details, allowing each layer to dry before adding the next. At the hinge of the cover (the spine edge), do not apply any paint layers thicker than 0.5 mm: this is where cracking starts. Use the thinnest possible paint at the hinge lines and keep design elements away from the hinge edge.
When the design is fully dry (allow overnight), apply a
of neat matte medium across the entire cover. Apply in thin, even strokes. The medium will look milky when wet and dry clear. One coat of medium is usually enough for a journal cover used in a bag.

items.symptom: The acrylic paint cracks at the cover hinge after a few weeks of use
items.cause: Paint was applied too thickly at the hinge line, and repeated flexing has cracked the rigid paint film.
items.fix: Flex cracks can be repaired by applying a thin coat of matte medium over the crack to re-seal the surface. For future covers, keep paint very thin at and near the hinge edge, or leave a 5 mm unpainted strip along the spine edge entirely.
